title.text: Generative AI: how chatbots write, and why they sometimes invent

objects.text: Why does a chatbot sound so sure, and when can I trust what it writes?

Leading with AI  |  Session 5 of the 15 (Sessions 0 to 14)
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. In Session 4 we saw AI that understands language: it sorts messages, finds a clause by meaning, translates and summarises. Today we move from AI that reads to AI that writes, the chatbots many of your staff already use. Our question: why does a chatbot sound so sure, and when can I trust what it writes?

We start in a New York court, build the idea from drawings, with no maths, look inside a real model’s choices, tour six industries, and see where chatbots help and where they invent. Then you add a drafting task of your own to your portfolio.

objects.text: By the end of today you will have

slides.notes:
By the end you will be able to explain how a chatbot writes, one word at a time, and why the same question can get two different answers. You will know where chatbots invent, citations, figures, policies and names, and hold five questions to ask of any answer.

And your portfolio will gain one drafting task, with the person who checks it and signs.

title.text:
Your two hours: how chatbots write, where
they help and invent, then your own portfolio

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: I show recorded runs of a real model. You add a drafting task to your own portfolio.

slides.notes: Ten minutes to recall Session 4 and meet today’s question. Forty minutes on how a chatbot writes, then six industries, two good uses and the costly failures. Fifteen minutes of demonstration on recorded runs. A five-minute break. Ten minutes on your people and the questions to ask. Then twenty-five minutes on your own portfolio, five on your decision and ten to close. First, how today fits, and five words.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What are the four jobs AI does with language?
2.  How did search by meaning find the force majeure clause for a question about floods?
3.  Why is translation into Luganda weaker than into English?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 4. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. 

Question one. What are the four jobs AI does with language? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Sort, search by meaning, translate and summarise.

Question two. How did search by meaning find the force majeure clause for a question about floods? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Texts that mean the same sit close together on a map of meaning, so the question landed next to the clause with no word in common.

Question three. Why is translation into Luganda weaker than into English? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. Luganda has far less written text for a model to learn from: it is a low-resource language.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet has it.

title.text: What today builds on, and where it leads

objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14; the gold one is today.

Today uses text as meaning from Session 4 and checking what comes out from Session 3.

It adds how chatbots write; fluent is not true.

Session 6: who makes the models, and how to choose.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Word
What it means
Generative AI
AI that produces new text, images or sound, instead of sorting or finding what already exists.
Large language model
The engine inside a chatbot: a model trained on a huge library of text to choose the next word.
Token
A piece of text the model reads and writes: a whole word or part of one.
Temperature
A setting for how adventurous the choice of next word is: low plays safe, high takes long shots.
Hallucination
The industry’s name for a fluent answer that is false or invented, such as a court case that does not exist.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. We use every one of them before the end of the session.

Generative AI. AI that produces new text, images or sound, instead of sorting or finding what already exists.

Large language model. The engine inside a chatbot: a model trained on a huge library of text to choose the next word.

Token. A piece of text the model reads and writes: a whole word or part of one.

Temperature. A setting for how adventurous the choice of next word is: low plays safe, high takes long shots.

Hallucination. The industry’s name for a fluent answer that is false or invented, such as a court case that does not exist.

title.text:
Session 4’s tools found text that already
existed; a chatbot writes text that never did

objects.alt: Session 4’s tools found text that already existed; a chatbot writes text that never did

objects.text: A found passage can be checked against its source. New text has no source to check against.

runs.text: The force majeure clause was in the contract.
A drafted reply exists nowhere until it is written.
So someone has to check it.

slides.notes:
Those five words mark a turn in the course. On the left is Session 4: you asked about a flooded road, the question was placed on the map of meaning, and the search returned a passage that already existed, the force majeure clause. You could hold it up against the contract.

On the right is today. You ask a chatbot to write a reply to a customer, and it produces new text, one word at a time, that never existed before. It may be right and it may be wrong, and that difference changes how a leader must treat the output. It has already cost people money in court.

title.text:
In New York in 2023 a chatbot invented court
cases, insisted one was real, and the lawyers paid

objects.alt: In New York in 2023 a chatbot invented court cases, insisted one was real, and the lawyers paid

objects.text: Why did it sound so sure, and when can you trust what it writes? That is today’s question.

runs.text: The cases did not exist.
Asked, it still said one was real.
The court held the people responsible.

slides.notes:
In 2023 a lawyer in New York, working on a case against the airline Avianca, asked ChatGPT for court decisions to cite. It produced decisions that did not exist, with quotations. When the lawyer asked whether one was real, it said the case does indeed exist. The court fined the two lawyers and their firm 5,000 US dollars and ordered them to write to their client and to each real judge named as the author of a fake opinion.

The tool sounded certain the whole way through. By the end of the session you should be able to explain why, and what to do about it.

title.text:
A chatbot writes one word at a time, like
phone autocomplete trained on a library

objects.alt: A chatbot writes one word at a time, like phone autocomplete trained on a library

objects.text: Your phone suggests the next word. A chatbot does the same thing thousands of times over.

runs.text: It adds the word, rereads, and chooses again.
It stops when the answer looks complete.
The engine is called a large language model.

slides.notes:
Start with something in your pocket. Type thank you for your on a phone, and it suggests the next word. These three suggestions are real: a small model, GPT-2, ranked support first, then continued, then patience. A chatbot does the same thing over and over. It chooses a likely next word, adds it to the text, reads the whole text again and chooses the next one, until the answer is complete.

The difference is scale. Your phone learned from your own messages, while a chatbot learned from a vast library of books, websites and articles. The industry calls the engine a large language model.

title.text:
At each step it ranks every possible
next word by how likely it is

objects.alt: At each step it ranks every possible next word by how likely it is

objects.text: Recorded from a real model: after “Thank you for your”, support leads with 30%.

runs.text: Every one of 50,257 pieces gets a share.
The top ten hold about two thirds.
There is no column for true or false.

slides.notes:
This is what the model sees, recorded from GPT-2. After thank you for your, every one of its 50,257 possible pieces gets a share of the chance. Support leads with 30 per cent. Continued has 10, patience 5, then interest, help, time and the rest. The top ten together hold about two thirds, and tens of thousands of other pieces share the remaining third.

Everything on this list is a word that tends to follow these words in the library. Nothing on it says whether the sentence will be true, and nothing checks it against your company’s records.

title.text:
It reads pieces of words, and our
languages are cut into more pieces

objects.alt: It reads pieces of words, and our languages are cut into more pieces

objects.text: The pieces are called tokens. Swahili needs nearly three per word.

runs.text: Many services charge by the piece.
Finer cutting means higher cost.
It also means weaker knowledge.

slides.notes:
A model does not read whole words. It reads pieces, which the industry calls tokens. In this example from GPT-2, Nile Valley Foods delivers maize flour to Mbale is eight words and eleven pieces. Nile splits into N and ile, Mbale into Mb and ale. The Swahili sentence habari, tunataka sukari magunia kumi, hello, we want ten sacks of sugar, is five words and fourteen pieces.

This links back to Session 4. Languages with less text are cut finer, so they cost more to process, since services are often priced by the piece, and the model knows them less well.

title.text:
It learned by guessing the next word across
a huge library, then was taught to be helpful

objects.alt: It learned by guessing the next word across a huge library, then was taught to be helpful

objects.text: Two steps of training, and neither checks facts.

runs.text: The same learning from examples as Session 0.
The second step makes it a chatbot.
Session 6 covers who does this training.

slides.notes:
The ranked lists come from training, the same learning from examples we met in Session 0. In the first step, the model reads a huge library, and at every point it hides the next word, guesses it, checks the real word, and adjusts itself to guess better. Repeated across books, websites and articles, that teaches it how language usually continues.

In the second step, people train it to follow instructions and give helpful answers, which is what makes it a chatbot. Session 6 says more about who does this. Neither step teaches it to check whether a sentence is true. It learns to sound like a good answer.

title.text:
It draws the next word like a raffle, so the
same question can get different answers

objects.alt: It draws the next word like a raffle, so the same question can get different answers

objects.text: Likely words hold more tickets. A long shot can still win.

runs.text: Each word is a fresh draw.
Low temperature: safe and repetitive.
High temperature: varied, then nonsense.

slides.notes:
Turn the ranked list into a raffle. The drum holds 100 tickets: support has 30, continued 10, patience 5, and all the other words share the rest. The model draws one ticket, adds that word, and holds a new raffle for the next. Ask the same question twice and you can get two different answers, because the draws differ.

A setting called temperature controls the raffle. At a low setting the favourite nearly always wins, so answers are safe and repetitive. At a high setting long shots win more often, so answers are varied, and eventually nonsense. You will see all three in the demonstration. Even the favourite word can be wrong, though.

title.text:
Asked where a fictional Jinja company is
based, the model suggests American cities

objects.alt: Asked where a fictional Jinja company is based, the model suggests American cities

objects.text: It ranks what sounds right. Nothing inside checks the facts.

runs.text: It never says “I do not know”.
Kampala starts only seventh for Uganda’s capital.
Newer models are better at facts; the mechanism is the same.

slides.notes:
This is the picture to remember from today, recorded from GPT-2. I wrote: Nile Valley Foods is a food distributor based in. The company is fictional, and in our story it sits in Jinja. The model has never heard of it, yet it does not say I do not know.

It ranks the, then San, Los, Salt and California: the beginnings of American city names, because that is how such sentences usually continue in its library. On the right, the capital of Uganda is: Kamp, the start of Kampala, comes only seventh. GPT-2 is a small 2019 model, and today’s chatbots are far better at facts. They still choose the word that sounds right.

title.text:
Chatbots invent citations, figures,
policies and names that look real

objects.alt: Chatbots invent citations, figures, policies and names that look real

objects.text: The more specific it looks, the more you should check it.

runs.text: The industry calls this hallucination.
Each kind has a document to check against.
Check before anything leaves the building.

slides.notes:
It invents in four places, and each looks convincing. Citations and court cases: case names, judges and quotations, as in New York. Figures and statistics: percentages, totals and dates with no source. Policies and promises: a refund rule or a discount your company never offered. And names, studies and sources: authors and reports that were never written.

The industry calls this hallucination. Each of the four has something you can check it against: the law report or ULII, your own records, the written policy, the original document. For a leader the rule is short: the more specific an answer looks, the more you check it.

title.text:
Chatbots are good at first drafts and
summaries, and weak on facts nobody checks

objects.alt: Chatbots are good at first drafts and summaries, and weak on facts nobody checks

objects.text: Use it to draft. Keep a person on the facts and the signature.

runs.text: It has never seen your company.
Its library stops at a date.
Session 8 gives it your documents.

slides.notes:
Put together, the pictures tell you where chatbots earn their keep. They are good at first drafts of letters, replies and reports, at summarising documents you also hold, at rewording for a reader, simpler, shorter or kinder, and at answering from documents you supply, which Session 8 builds on.

They are weak at facts, figures and citations drawn from memory, at recent events and at your own company, which they have never seen, and at saying I do not know. Anything signed without a person checking is a risk you chose to take.

title.text:
Banks, telcos, farms, offices, clinics and
schools already put chatbots to work

objects.alt: Banks, telcos, farms, offices, clinics and schools already put chatbots to work

objects.text: Klarna’s and Nestlé’s figures are their own; Vodacom’s is an announcement with no results yet.

slides.notes:
In banking, Klarna says its assistant took two-thirds of customer chats in its first month, a company figure, and in 2025 it began hiring people again because quality fell; Session 12 tells that story. In telecom, Vodacom announced plans in 2025 to use chatbots in customer care, with no results yet.

In agriculture, Farmer.Chat answers farmers in their own languages. In FMCG, Nestlé gave office staff their own assistant for drafting; staff estimated 45 minutes saved a week. In health, Penda Health’s safety net, from Session 0, reads clinicians’ notes and flags possible errors; clinicians with it made 16 per cent fewer diagnostic errors.

In the public sector, Edo State in Nigeria used a chatbot as an English tutor.

title.text:
Edo State pupils tutored by a chatbot, with teachers
in the room, gained nearly two years in six weeks

objects.alt: Edo State pupils tutored by a chatbot, with teachers in the room, gained nearly two years in six weeks

objects.text: Pupils were picked at random to take part and compared with pupils who did not.

slides.notes:
The first good use is in education, and it was properly tested. In Edo State, Nigeria, pupils worked in pairs with a chatbot as an after-school English tutor, twice a week for six weeks, with teachers in the room setting the topic, the prompts and the reflection. Pupils were picked at random to take part, and compared with those who were not.

The World Bank reports that the gain equals nearly two years of typical learning, better than 80 per cent of education programmes tested in developing countries, and girls gained more. Hold it loosely: it was a six-week pilot, the two years is a comparison, and the teachers made it work.

title.text:
Farmer.Chat answers farmers only from checked
advice, and leaves a quarter of questions unanswered

objects.alt: Farmer.Chat answers farmers only from checked advice, and leaves a quarter of questions unanswered

slides.notes:
The second good use is in agriculture. Farmers have questions every day, extension workers are few, and much advice is not in their language. Farmer.Chat, from Digital Green, answers by text, voice or photo, in local languages, and it draws only on a library of farming content that experts checked, which keeps it close to the facts.

By 2024 more than 15,000 users had asked over 300,000 questions, most of them in Kenya. It answered about three in four, and about eight in ten answers stuck closely to the checked content. One question in four went unanswered, mostly because the library had gaps. Session 8 returns to that design.

title.text:
Invented citations reached courts in New York and
KwaZulu-Natal, and a government report in Australia

objects.alt: Invented citations reached courts in New York and KwaZulu-Natal, and a government report in Australia

slides.notes:
The failures repeat. New York, June 2023, you know: invented cases, a 5,000 dollar penalty. In South Africa, in January 2025, the KwaZulu-Natal High Court found that only two of the nine cases a legal team had cited could be found, suspected an AI tool, ordered costs and referred the lawyers to the Legal Practice Council.

In Australia in 2025, a Deloitte report to a government department, a contract worth 440,000 Australian dollars, turned out to contain fake references and a made-up court quotation. In October, Deloitte agreed to repay the final instalment. In all three, a person signed what a machine had written without checking it.

title.text:
Air Canada paid for its chatbot’s wrong
answer, and DPD switched its bot off

objects.alt: Air Canada paid for its chatbot’s wrong answer, and DPD switched its bot off

slides.notes:
The same holds for chatbots that talk to customers. A grieving passenger asked Air Canada’s website chatbot about bereavement fares, and it wrongly said the discount could be claimed after travel. The airline argued that the chatbot was responsible for its own words. The tribunal disagreed: the chatbot is part of your website, and the airline paid about 812 Canadian dollars.

The sum was small and the principle is large. In the UK, after a system update, a frustrated customer got the parcel firm DPD’s chatbot to swear and mock the company, and the screenshots spread widely. DPD switched the AI part off. A chatbot on your website speaks for you.

title.text:
A small model at three settings, then a
current assistant asked about a fake case

objects.text: I will show

runs.text: GPT-2 finishes one sentence six times at each of three settings.
Claude is asked twice about a court case and studies that do not exist.

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: How the same prompt changes with the setting
Fluent text that contradicts itself
What the assistant does with a case that does not exist

slides.notes:
Two recorded demonstrations. First, I gave GPT-2, a small open model you can run on a laptop, the start of a sentence: the customer was angry because the delivery was. It wrote fourteen more pieces, six times at each of three temperature settings, recorded on 6 November 2026.

Second, I asked a current assistant, Claude, in two fresh sessions on 4 November 2026, about a court case that does not exist. Watch how the text changes with the setting, look for fluent text that contradicts itself, and see what the assistant does with the false case. Neither is ChatGPT or Gemini, and behaviour differs between tools.

title.text:
At a low setting it repeats itself, in the middle it
contradicts itself, and at high it writes nonsense

objects.alt: At a low setting it repeats itself, in the middle it contradicts itself, and at high it writes nonsense

slides.notes:
At the low setting the favourite word wins almost every time: delayed, delayed, delayed, and it even repeats its own sentence. Safe, and dull. At the middle setting the answers vary, and the gold one reads: the customer was angry because the delivery was very extremely fast and arrived in a timely manner, and the service was excellent.

Perfectly fluent, and it contradicts the start of its own sentence. At the high setting the long shots win and it becomes nonsense. Your chatbot’s supplier chooses this setting, and some tools let you change it. The second run matters more for your organisation.

title.text:
Asked about a court case that does not exist, a current
assistant declined both times, in different words

objects.alt: Asked about a court case that does not exist, a current assistant declined both times, in different words

slides.notes:
I asked which court decided Nile Valley Foods against the Commissioner General of the Uganda Revenue Authority in 2019, with the citation, and for three published studies on WhatsApp orders in Ugandan wholesale. The case and the company are invented. In both runs the assistant declined: I can’t confirm that this case exists, and I have no record of a case with that name, and I won’t guess.

It named no studies, and pointed to ULII and the Tax Appeals Tribunal. The two answers agree in substance and differ in wording, which is the raffle again. Two good runs of one tool prove little, though. The New York lawyers’ tool invented.

title.text:
Five questions to ask of any
chatbot answer before you use it

objects.alt: Five questions to ask of any chatbot answer before you use it

objects.text: Ask them of every answer that leaves the building.

runs.text: Two answers that disagree cannot both be right.
Question five is Session 3’s cost of a mistake.
All five are on your take-away sheet.

slides.notes:
Carry five questions out of the demonstration. One: where did this come from, and can I open the source?

Two: do the names, numbers and citations check out, each one?

Three: would it say the same if I asked again, since two answers that disagree cannot both be trusted?

Four: did it answer from our own documents, or from its memory of the library?

Five: what does it cost if it is wrong, and who signs?

That last one comes from Session 3’s cost of a mistake. The five are on your take-away sheet, and they are also what your people now need to learn.

title.text:
Everyone drafts with it now, so the
skill your people need is checking

objects.alt: Everyone drafts with it now, so the skill your people need is checking

objects.text: Nestlé staff estimate 45 minutes a week saved; Klarna rehired people when quality fell.

slides.notes:
Chatbots touch almost every desk. A legal or compliance officer drafts letters and memos faster, and now checks every citation and clause, because Mavundla and New York show what happens otherwise. A customer service agent stops typing the same reply again and again, handles the hard cases and checks the drafts, and needs to know company policy cold, to catch an Air Canada promise.

Analysts and report writers lose the blank page and spend their time on sources, figures and judgement. The fears are real: being blamed for the bot, being replaced, work that looks generic. What do your staff fear, and are they already using these tools without telling you?

title.text:
The machine drafts; a named person checks
and signs, and the organisation answers

objects.alt: The machine drafts; a named person checks and signs, and the organisation answers

objects.text: Write down who checks and who signs before anyone uses it for real.

runs.text: Deloitte’s corrected report disclosed its AI use.
The same chain as Session 2’s credit score.
Agree which documents need a second check.

slides.notes:
Whatever your people fear, one rule protects them and your customers. The machine drafts the reply, the report or the summary. A person checks the facts, figures, sources and tone. A named person signs, and says where it matters that AI helped; Deloitte’s corrected report disclosed its AI use.

And the organisation answers, to the customer, the court or the regulator, as Air Canada found. This is the same chain as Session 2, where the score supported the decision and a named person owned it. Write it down before anyone uses a chatbot for real work, and agree which documents need a second check.

title.text:
Before you trust a chatbot, find out where your data
goes and how often it invents on your questions

rows.text: Ask
Why it matters
Where do our prompts and documents go, and are they kept?
Staff paste in customer and company data
Can it answer from our own documents and show the source?
Answers from memory invent more
How often does it invent on our kind of questions?
Test it on twenty questions with known answers
Who checks and signs what it drafts?
The organisation answers for it
What happens when it does not know?
A good tool says so, and routes to a person
Who tests it again after each update?
DPD’s bot changed after an update

slides.notes:
Everything so far comes down to six questions for your team and your supplier. Ask where your prompts and documents go and whether they are kept, because staff paste in customer and company data; Session 6 takes that further. Ask whether it can answer from your own documents and show the source, because answers from memory invent more.

Ask how often it invents on your kind of questions, and test it on twenty with known answers. Ask who checks and signs. Ask what it does when it does not know: a good tool says so and routes to a person. And ask who tests it again after each update, as DPD learned.

title.text:
Add one drafting task to your AI Opportunity
Portfolio, with the person who signs

objects.text: 25 minutes
Hands-on: your portfolio
Choose a writing task your staff repeat every week.

runs.text: Name the task: replies, reports, minutes or letters.
Fill the five columns, as in the example.
Add today’s column: the checks, and who signs.
Mark which of the four invention risks apply.

objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: One drafting task, with its checks and the person who signs.

slides.notes:
For twenty-five minutes you work on your own organisation, and I walk round. Choose a writing task your staff repeat every week: replies to customers, monthly reports, minutes, letters to suppliers. Open the AI Opportunity Portfolio in your workbook and fill the five columns: the use, what goes in, what comes out, who uses it, and how you would know it works.

Then today’s column: what a person must check, and who signs. Mark which of the four invention risks apply. The example on the right is for Nile Valley Foods, our fictional distributor. A good first task is one where a mistake is cheap and easy to spot.

title.text:
Which drafting task would
you hand to a chatbot first?

objects.text: Of the tasks you just wrote down, which would you start with, and why?

objects.alt: mail

objects.text: Draft replies
Letters and messages to customers, checked before sending

objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Sum up reports
Long reports and minutes for busy managers, with the original kept

objects.alt: folder

objects.text: Staff questions
First answers from our own policies, with the source shown

objects.alt: clock

objects.text: Not yet
We have no rule on who checks and signs, or where data goes
Write your decision and the reason in your workbook.

slides.notes:
With your entries written, one decision: which drafting task would you hand to a chatbot first?

Draft replies, if your staff type similar letters and messages all day; a person checks before anything is sent. Sum up reports, if your managers drown in reports and minutes; the original stays to hand. Staff questions, if people keep asking HR or finance the same things; the answers should come from your own policies, which Session 8 shows how to do.

Or not yet, if you have no rule on who checks and signs or where the data goes. That is a fair answer, and Session 13 helps you write the rule. I will ask three of you for your choice and who signs.

title.text:
A chatbot writes the likely word, so a
named person checks the facts and signs

objects.alt: A chatbot writes the likely word, so a named person checks the facts and signs

objects.text: Fluent text with nothing inside checking it.

runs.text: Answers vary because each word is a draw.
Check citations, figures, policies and names first.
The organisation answers for what it sends.

slides.notes:
If you keep one picture from today, keep this one: a model placing a Jinja company in American cities without a moment’s doubt. A chatbot writes one likely word at a time, like autocomplete trained on a library, and draws each word like a raffle, so the same question can get different answers; temperature makes it safer or wilder.

Nothing inside checks the facts. It invents where things look most specific, citations, figures, policies and names, so check those first. A named person signs, because the organisation answers for what its chatbot writes, as Air Canada and the courts found.

title.text:
Keep the sheet, and the drafting
task you added to your portfolio

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A one-page sheet: how a chatbot writes, why answers vary, where it invents, the five questions to ask of any answer, today’s recorded runs, and your new portfolio entry.

objects.text: Our question today
Why does a chatbot sound so sure, and when can I trust what it writes?
Next session
Session 6: The AI market: models, vendors, and buy, rent or build.

objects.alt: What you keep from today

slides.notes:
The take-away sheet shows the picture of a chatbot writing one likely word at a time, the raffle that explains why answers vary, the four places it invents, and the five questions to ask of any answer. It also has today’s recorded runs: the support list, American cities for a company in Jinja, and two careful answers about a court case that does not exist.

Your portfolio now holds a drafting task and the person who signs. In Session 6 we ask who makes these models, where your data goes, and how to choose a supplier.

We began with this question: Why does a chatbot sound so sure, and when can I trust what it writes? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
